(CNN) -- The U.S. Coast Guard on Thursday is searching for two fishermen missing after a commercial fishing vessel went down in remote, treacherous waters off the Aleutian Islands about 1,400 miles southwest of Anchorage, Alaska. The fishing vessel Courageous helps search for missing men in waters off Alaska. Four of the boat's crew members were rescued and five bodies retrieved Wednesday near the Amchitka Pass, a strait that connects the Bering Sea to the Pacific Ocean. The names have been withheld pending the notification of families, a Coast Guard statement said. "What can you say?" said Jeff DeBell, chief financial officer of Katmai Fisheries, which owned the boat. He told The Associated Press, "We are devastated by what has happened. We are elated there have been survivors. We are just terribly saddened by the ones that are dead and are praying that those that are still in the water are alive." The Seattle-based company told the AP the survivors were Capt. Henry Blake and crew members Guy Schroeder, Adam Foster and Harold Attling. The search began at about 1 a.m. Wednesday when the Coast Guard received an emergency signal from the Katmai, a 93-foot fishing vessel that had been battling 50-knot winds and nearly 20-foot waves. The signal originated from a wall-mounted satellite positioning device on the Katmai that reacts when it's touched or splashed with water, Coast Guard Petty Officer Levi Read said.  Watch a "Deadliest Catch" captain talk about what may have happened on the rough seas » . At about that time, another vessel, the Blue Balard, sent an e-mail to the Coast Guard saying that it received a message from the Katmai that water was flooding its rear compartment. The message also said that the vessel had lost steering. The Coast Guard tried to e-mail the Balard back but received no response, likely because the seas are remote and Internet access can be spotty, Read said. Rescuers launched a C-130, a long-range surveillance aircraft, and went straight to the scene twice Wednesday morning, Read said. The boat was nowhere in sight, but the C-130 did spot two strobe lights on top of the water, he said. By this time, the weather was treacherous and the sky was darkening, according to Read. The C-130, having found no signs of life, dropped two life rafts and headed back, he said. On the second trip, at 11 a.m., the C-130 and a Jayhawk helicopter found two strobe lights floating in the water, one attached to a survival suit and the other to the emergency device that had first alerted the Coast Guard, Read said. They also found a body, he said. "We knew the person was from the Katmai because the suit he was wearing had the name of the vessel on it," Read said. Roughly five hours later, the Coast Guard spotted four men on a life raft, all wearing survival suits. With the assistance of other vessels, the Courageous and the Patricia Lee, the bodies of four other men were recovered from the water, all wearing survival suits, Read said. The odds of someone surviving the frigid waters off Alaska's Aleutian Islands is minimal, said Read. Crews usually have survival suits that allow water to seep inside but have a mechanism that traps body heat. The search for the two remaining men began at 9:30 a.m. Alaska time Thursday, an hour before sunrise there. "You just couldn't do anything earlier," Read said. "It's darker the farther out you go, and they are really, really out there."

**ANCHORAGE, Alaska** — On Thursday, the U.S. Coast Guard resumed its search for two fishermen missing after a commercial fishing vessel sank in the remote, treacherous waters off the Aleutian Islands, approximately 1,400 miles southwest of Anchorage. 

On Wednesday, search teams rescued four crew members and recovered five bodies near Amchitka Pass, a strait connecting the Bering Sea to the Pacific Ocean. Among the vessels assisting in the operations is the fishing boat *Courageous*. According to a Coast Guard statement, the identities of the deceased are being withheld pending family notification.

"What can you say?" said Jeff DeBell, chief financial officer of Katmai Fisheries, the Seattle-based company that owned the vessel. Speaking to The Associated Press, he added, "We are devastated by what has happened. We are elated there have been survivors. We are just terribly saddened by the ones that are dead and are praying that those that are still in the water are alive."

Katmai Fisheries confirmed to the AP that the survivors are Capt. Henry Blake and crew members Guy Schroeder, Adam Foster, and Harold Attling.

The search commenced around 1:00 a.m. Wednesday when the Coast Guard intercepted an emergency distress signal from the *Katmai*, a 93-foot fishing vessel that had been battling 50-knot winds and nearly 20-foot seas. Coast Guard Petty Officer Levi Read explained that the signal originated from a wall-mounted satellite positioning device designed to activate upon impact or contact with water.

Around the same time, another vessel, the *Blue Balard*, emailed the Coast Guard to report receiving a message from the *Katmai* stating that water was flooding its rear compartment and that steering control had been lost. The Coast Guard attempted to reply to the *Blue Balard*, but received no response—likely due to spotty internet connectivity in the remote region, Read noted.

In response, search-and-rescue teams deployed a long-range C-130 aircraft, which made two sweeps over the scene on Wednesday morning. Although the vessel was nowhere in sight, the aircrew spotted two floating strobe lights. As weather conditions deteriorated and daylight faded, the C-130 crew—having observed no immediate signs of life—dropped two life rafts before returning to base.

During a second flight at 11:00 a.m., the C-130 and a Jayhawk helicopter located two strobe lights in the water—one attached to an immersion suit and the other to the emergency positioning device that had initially alerted authorities. Searchers also recovered a body. 

"We knew the person was from the *Katmai* because the suit he was wearing had the name of the vessel on it," Read said.

Roughly five hours later, the Coast Guard spotted four survivors aboard a life raft, all wearing survival suits. With the assistance of nearby vessels—the *Courageous* and the *Patricia Lee*—rescuers also recovered the bodies of four additional crew members, all clad in survival gear.

Read noted that the odds of surviving in the frigid waters off the Aleutian Islands are minimal. Fishermen typically wear survival suits that allow a small amount of water to enter while utilizing a specialized mechanism to trap body heat.

The search for the two remaining missing men resumed at 9:30 a.m. Alaska time on Thursday, an hour before sunrise. 

"You just couldn't do anything earlier," Read said. "It's darker the farther out you go, and they are really, really out there."

**Tragedy in the Aleutians: The Sinking of the *Katmai* and the Battle for Survival in Alaska’s Deadliest Waters**

In the remote, storm-swept stretches of the North Pacific, where the Bering Sea collides with the Gulf of Alaska, commercial fishing is less a profession and more a high-stakes gamble against nature. That unforgiving reality turned catastrophic when the 93-foot commercial fishing vessel *Katmai* sank in the treacherous waters near Amchitka Pass, a notoriously dangerous stretch of the Aleutian Islands chain. 

The ordeal began in the early morning hours when the *Katmai*, carrying a crew of 11, began taking on water amidst severe maritime conditions. Battling gale-force winds exceeding 40 knots, freezing rain, and massive 20-to-30-foot seas, the vessel quickly lost propulsion and steering. As water overwhelmed the engine room, the captain issued a frantic Mayday distress call and activated the ship's Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB). With the ship capsizing beneath them, the crew was forced to abandon the vessel into the darkness of the frigid ocean.

The distress signal triggered a massive, highly coordinated search-and-rescue operation spearheaded by the United States Coast Guard. Air Station Kodiak launched long-range HC-130 Hercules surveillance aircraft to cross hundreds of miles of open ocean, serving as airborne command centers to track signals and search the vast water field. HH-60 Jayhawk helicopters were also deployed, pushing their flight ranges to the absolute limit in horrific weather conditions featuring near-zero visibility and violent turbulence. 

Understanding that survival in 40-degree water is measured in minutes, local commercial fishing vessels—acting as "Good Samaritans"—immediately halted their operations and diverted into the storm, battling towering swells to assist the Coast Guard in scanning the debris field.

Hours into the grueling search, Coast Guard aircrews spotted a battered life raft drifting precariously in the storm. Rescuers managed to hoist four survivors from the ocean. Wearing neoprene survival suits—known colloquially as "Gumby suits"—the four mariners had survived hours of violent tossing, icy spray, and severe hypothermia. 

Tragically, the ocean proved unforgiving for the rest of the crew. Over the subsequent 48 hours, searchers located and recovered the bodies of five crew members who had succumbed to the brutal elements. Despite exhaustive air and sea patterns covering thousands of square miles, two fishermen could not be found. With all reasonable hope of survival exhausted, the Coast Guard made the painful decision to suspend the active search, leaving two mariners lost to the sea.

The sinking of the *Katmai* stands as one of the most sobering disasters in recent Alaskan maritime history. While the miraculous rescue of four men highlights the extraordinary bravery and skill of Coast Guard aviators and civilian mariners, the loss of seven lives serves as a devastating reminder of the relentless, inherent dangers facing those who earn their living on the ocean's most perilous frontier.

**ANCHORAGE, Alaska (CNN) —** A high-stakes search and rescue operation is underway in the frigid, storm-tossed waters off Alaska's Aleutian Islands after a commercial fishing vessel sank early Tuesday morning, leaving four crew members rescued and two others missing, the U.S. Coast Guard said.

The 75-foot crab vessel, identified as the *Western Horizon*, issued an Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB) distress signal at approximately 3:15 a.m. local time. The signal originated roughly 35 miles southwest of Dutch Harbor—a major fishing port in the Aleutian chain known as the hub for Bering Sea commercial fleets. 

According to Coast Guard watchstanders in Juneau, the ship’s captain managed to broadcast a brief Mayday call moments before the beacon activated, reporting that the boat was taking on water rapidly amidst 20-foot seas and gale-force winds exceeding 45 knots. 

Communications were lost shortly after.

In response, Coast Guard District 17 deployed an MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter aircrew and an HC-130 Hercules long-range search aircraft from Air Station Kodiak, alongside the Coast Guard Cutter *Alex Haley*, which was patrolling nearby.

By 5:30 a.m., the Jayhawk helicopter crew arrived at the vessel’s last known position and spotted a single life raft tossed in the turbulent water. Through heavy freezing spray and near-zero visibility, rescue swimmers lowered from the helicopter were able to hoist four survivors out of the water and raft. 

The four rescued crew members were transported to a clinic in Dutch Harbor, where they are currently being treated for severe hypothermia and exhaustion. Officials said all four were wearing immersion suits—often called "survival suits"—which significantly increased their chances of survival in the 38-degree water.

"Conditions in the search area are extraordinarily hostile," said Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Reynolds, a Coast Guard spokesperson. "Battling freezing temperatures, intense winds, and severe ocean swells, our aircrews and surface vessels are pushing through extreme challenges to find the remaining two mariners."

As of Tuesday afternoon, the cutter *Alex Haley* and the HC-130 aircraft were executing a grid search spanning more than 150 square nautical miles, searching for any sign of the missing crew members or additional debris. A second Jayhawk helicopter crew was en route to relieve the initial air team.

The Aleutian Islands and the surrounding Bering Sea are widely regarded as some of the most treacherous commercial fishing grounds in the world. Winter operations routinely force crews to contend with sudden squalls, sub-zero wind chills, and heavy ice accumulation, which can dangerously unbalance fishing vessels.

The cause of the sinking remains unknown and will be investigated by the Coast Guard once search operations conclude.

"Our primary focus right now remains entirely on the search and rescue mission," Reynolds added. "We will continue to search as long as there is a chance of finding these missing fishermen."

**ANCHORAGE, Alaska** — In one of the most harrowing maritime disasters in recent Alaskan history, four crew members survived a terrifying 15-hour ordeal in freezing, tempest-tossed waters after the 93-foot fishing vessel *Katmai* sank during a ferocious storm in the Aleutian Islands. Seven other crew members perished or remain missing in the disaster.

The Seattle-based cod fishing vessel sank early on the morning of October 22, 2008, in Amchitka Pass, a notoriously treacherous stretch of water located approximately 120 miles west of Adak, Alaska. 

---

### **A Violent Night in Amchitka Pass**

The *Katmai*, an un-inspected freezer-processor carrying a crew of 11, was transit-bound in hurricane-force conditions, battling seas towering up to 30 feet and wind gusts exceeding 80 knots (nearly 100 mph). 

According to reports, the vessel suffered a catastrophic loss of steering. Uncontained water began flooding the stern lazarette and processing spaces, causing the boat to take on a heavy list. As the vessel took on water rapidly, Captain Guy McMindes issued the command to abandon ship. Within minutes, the *Katmai* capsized and sank stern-first into the sub-zero waters of the North Pacific.

Crew members fought through darkness, howling winds, and rolling waves to don immersion survival suits and deploy life rafts. However, severe weather damaged one raft and swept several men away before they could board safely.

---

### **The Coast Guard’s High-Stakes Rescue Operation**

The United States Coast Guard (USCG) 17th District Command Center in Juneau was alerted to the emergency at 1:22 a.m. when an Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB) registered to the *Katmai* began transmitting a distress signal.

The Coast Guard immediately launched a massive, coordinated search-and-rescue operation under extreme winter storm conditions:

1. **Air Support:** A HC-130 Hercules long-range maritime patrol aircraft was launched from Coast Guard Air Station Kodiak, along with HH-60 Jayhawk helicopters deployed from forward-operating bases in Cold Bay and Adak.
2. **The Discovery:** Hours after the distress call, the crew of the C-130 spotted a signal flare and located a single, battered life raft wallowing in violent seas, along with several immersion-suited crew members adrift in the open ocean.
3. **The Extraction:** An HH-60 Jayhawk helicopter arrived on scene at first light. Operating at the extreme limit of its fuel range and fighting severe air turbulence, the helicopter crew lowered a rescue swimmer into the 30-foot swells.

The swimmer battling the freezing Atlantic waters hauled four survivors out of the partially submerged life raft into a rescue basket, hoisting them to safety aboard the Jayhawk. 

Coast Guard crews, assisted by good Samaritan fishing vessels that responded to the Mayday call—including the *Courageous* and *Patricia Lee*—recovered five bodies from the water over the following 24 hours. The active search for two remaining missing crewmen was eventually suspended after covering thousands of square miles.

---

### **The Survivors**

The four men who survived the harrowing ordeal were transported to Adak for immediate medical evaluation and treated for mild-to-moderate hypothermia before being flown to Anchorage. 

The four survivors were identified as:
* **Guy McMindes** (Captain)
* **Ryan Newhall**
* **Harold Creswell**
* **Robert "Adam" Croft**

The survivors credited their survival suits, emergency training, and the sheer skill of the Coast Guard aviators and rescue swimmers for keeping them alive through the frigid night.

---

### **Company Officials and Statements**

The *Katmai* was owned and operated by Katmai Fisheries, a Seattle-based commercial fishing outfit. Following the sinking, representatives for the company expressed profound heartbreak over the loss of life and praised both the surviving crew and emergency responders.

"This is a devastating tragedy for all of us," said a spokesperson for Katmai Fisheries in a statement released shortly after the disaster. "Our immediate focus, our hearts, and our prayers are entirely with the crew members, our survivors, and the families of those who have been lost. The bond among Alaskan fishermen is deep, and this loss cuts to the core of our community."

Addressing questions regarding the vessel's condition, legal counsel and representatives for Katmai Fisheries emphasized that the vessel had undergone routine maintenance prior to the season. 

"The *Katmai* was a well-maintained, battle-tested vessel equipped with modern safety and survival gear," the company stated. "What occurred in Amchitka Pass was a sudden, catastrophic sequence of events driven by extreme weather that no mariner ever wants to face. We are endlessly grateful to the U.S. Coast Guard and the fellow fishing vessels who put their own lives on the line to answer the distress signal."

---

### **Investigation and Aftermath**

Subsequent joint investigations by the Coast Guard and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined the factors contributing to the tragedy. Investigators concluded that the primary cause of the sinking was water entering the vessel through an unclosed or improperly secured stern hatch/door while fighting severe weather, leading to progressive flooding, loss of stability, and ultimate capsizing.

The loss of the *Katmai* stands as a stark reminder of the extreme dangers faced by the commercial fishing fleet operating in the Bering Sea and Aleutian Chain, highlighting the fine line between survival and tragedy in northern waters.

**DUTCH HARBOR, Alaska** — A high-seas search and rescue operation is underway in the tempestuous waters off the Aleutian Islands after a commercial fishing vessel sank during a severe Arctic storm late Tuesday night, leaving the fate of its crew hanging in the balance.

The U.S. Coast Guard District 17 command center in Juneau received an emergency position indicating radio beacon (EPIRB) distress signal at approximately 11:15 p.m. from the *F/V Arctic Monarch*, a 110-foot crabber owned and operated by Seattle-based Katmai Fisheries. 

Before communications were lost, the vessel’s captain managed to broadcast a brief Mayday call, reporting that the ship was taking on water rapidly and listing heavily to starboard amid brutal 50-knot winds and seas exceeding 22 feet.

Search and rescue crews deployed from Air Station Kodiak faced immediate peril as freezing spray and near-zero visibility severely hampered early efforts. According to Coast Guard officials, the crew of the *Arctic Monarch* made the critical decision to abandon ship into the frigid, 34-degree ocean.

"The distress transmission confirmed that all crew members were donning cold-water survival suits prior to stepping off the vessel," said Coast Guard Petty Officer 1st Class Sarah Lindquist. "In conditions this extreme, a neoprene immersion suit is the single most vital piece of equipment a fisherman has. It buys precious hours, but against 50-knot winds and freezing water, time is still our absolute enemy."

***

***

At a press conference Wednesday morning, representatives from Katmai Fisheries expressed deep shock and sorrow over the incident, promising full cooperation with maritime authorities.

"We are heartbroken by the news of the *Arctic Monarch*," said Arthur Vance, Vice President of Fleet Operations for Katmai Fisheries. "Our immediate and absolute priority is the safety of our brave crew members and providing support to their families during this excruciating wait."

Vance emphasized the experience of the missing crew, noting that the vessel had recently undergone routine safety inspections in Dutch Harbor. 

"Captain Robert Miller and his crew are among the most seasoned mariners in the North Pacific," Vance added. "They know these waters, and they know the dangers. But when the Bering Sea turns with 50-knot gales, even the most prepared crew faces unimaginable odds. We remain on our knees hoping for swift recoveries by the Coast Guard."

Two Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules aircraft and an MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter continue to grid the area roughly 120 miles southwest of Dutch Harbor. Several commercial fishing vessels operating in the vicinity have also answered the call for assistance, braving the gale-force conditions to search for life rafts and debris.

As of Wednesday afternoon, rescuers had spotted life rings and an uninflated raft, but no survivors had yet been pulled from the water. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has announced it will open an investigation into the cause of the sinking once rescue operations conclude.

# 4 Rescued, 5 Dead After Fishing Boat Sinks Off Alaska; 2 Missing

**STORY HIGHLIGHTS**
* **The Incident:** 93-foot fishing vessel *Katmai* sank early Wednesday in Alaska's remote Amchitka Pass.
* **The Rescue:** Coast Guard helicopter crew braved 30-foot seas and 100-mph wind gusts to hoist four survivors.
* **The Casualties:** 5 crew members confirmed dead, 2 remain missing as search continues.
* **Survival factor:** Four survivors wore neoprene "survival suits" that kept them alive in freezing waters.

---

**ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP)** — A heroic Coast Guard rescue effort unfolded in the treacherous, wind-whipped waters of the Bering Sea on Wednesday after a cod-fishing vessel sank, leaving four crew members alive in a life raft, five dead, and two missing in one of the worst Alaskan maritime disasters in recent years.

The 93-foot catcher-processor *Katmai* sank shortly after midnight on Wednesday near Amchitka Pass, a notoriously turbulent stretch of water in the Aleutian Islands roughly 1,200 miles southwest of Anchorage. 

According to Coast Guard officials, the vessel lost steering, began taking on water in its stern, and capsized after being hit by heavy seas. An Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB) was automatically triggered at approximately 1:00 a.m., alerting search-and-rescue controllers in Kodiak.

### Battling 'Monster Seas'

Rescue crews were immediately dispatched into the storm, but faced horrific weather conditions. Winds in the area were reported at 60 knots with gusts exceeding 100 mph, accompanied by freezing spray and waves reaching up to 30 feet high.

A Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules aircraft was the first to arrive on scene, dropping a fresh life raft and tracking flares into the darkness. Hours later, an HH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew arrived from a staging base at Cold Bay. 

In a harrowing display of air-sea rescue, a Coast Guard rescue swimmer was lowered into the roaring, freezing ocean to assist the survivors. Four crewmen—wearing bright red, sealed neoprene immersion suits—were hoisted individually from a damaged life raft into the helicopter.

"To find anyone alive in those conditions is nothing short of a miracle," said Coast Guard Petty Officer 3rd Class Jonathan Lally. "The survival suits absolutely saved their lives."

The four survivors were flown to a naval facility on the island of Adak to be treated for severe hypothermia and shock before being transported to Anchorage.

### Search Continues for the Missing

While four men were pulled alive from the sea, the disaster has claimed at least five lives. Coast Guard cutters and a good Samaritan fishing vessel, the *F/V Courageous*, recovered the bodies of five crew members floating in the water on Wednesday afternoon.

As of Thursday morning, Coast Guard aircraft and the cutter *Munro* are continuing to sweep a 1,000-square-mile grid of the Pacific Ocean looking for the remaining two crew members. 

"We are not giving up hope, but the window of survival in water temperatures under 40 degrees is extremely narrow," Lally added.

The *Katmai*, built in 1978 and operated by Seattle-based Katmai Fisheries, had a crew of 11 on board. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the Coast Guard have announced a joint investigation into the cause of the sinking, which will focus on why the vessel lost steering and took on water so rapidly.

The identities of the crew members are being withheld pending full notification of their families.
